To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HIT systems designed to improve care should be designed with the following characteristics in mind: they should provide information in a way that is relevant and useful to clinicians; they should provide information that clinicians can easily integrate into their current workflow; they should be designed in a way that clinicians can use the system to make decisions about care; and they should be designed to be flexible and adaptable.

1) HIT systems are a promising tool for improving clinical practice; 2) HIT systems can be used to provide clinical decision support to physicians, but this is only a first step; 3) HIT systems can help physicians and patients make more informed decisions, but this requires a system that is designed to support a patient-centered care process; 4) a patient-centered HIT system can be designed to help patients and their physicians make more informed decisions and to help patients take more responsibility for their

HIT tools can be designed to catalyze change in clinical care; and the design of these tools should be informed by an understanding of the clinical context, the nature and characteristics of the clinical problem, and the cognitive processes of the user.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of effective and usable disease management HIT systems that can be used to improve the quality of care.
the design of HIT systems that are more closely integrated into the existing work flow, more closely tied to clinical decision-making and more closely tied to financial incentives.
the design of HIT tools that will catalyse change, and that will support clinical decision making in the context of a complex and changing environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a lack of evidence to support the use of HIT for disease management.
the evidence for the effectiveness of HIT is limited and that the design of HIT systems needs to be more carefully considered to improve the likelihood of success.
HIT can be designed in a way that can improve clinical care, but this is not always the case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIT systems should be designed to be more than a repository of information.

the design of HIT to catalyse clinical change must be based on a thorough understanding of the clinical problem, the workflow, the cognitive processes and the culture within which the HIT will be used.
HIT can be designed to support the clinician in the process of care, and can also be used to support the organisation of care.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of HIT tools for disease management should be guided by an explicit conceptual framework that takes into account the social and organisational context in which they are implemented.
HIT systems should be developed with the goal of catalysing change in clinical care, not simply to improve the quality of information.
HIT tools must be designed to catalyse changes in workflow, not just changes in behaviour.
